title: Clean air needs targets, timelines, accountability
syllabus: GS3 › Environmental pollution and degradation · GS2 › Government policies and interventions; Inter-ministerial coordination · GS4 › Accountability; form versus substance
summary: Clean-air policy rewards paperwork, not cleaner air; as India drafts NCAP 2.0, the writer wants success measured by reduced exposure, with deadlines and accountability across departments.
evolution: National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) launched for cities that fail air quality standards.
Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan ranks Lucknow India's best million-plus city, yet its PM10 is still over twice the safe standard.
CREA finds no appreciable improvement in Delhi's winter air over four years, despite GRAP.
ideas: Seasonal amnesia: toxic air returns every winter, draws outrage, then is forgotten.
GS3 · Air pollution (introduction)
India's response to air pollution suffers from 'seasonal amnesia': outrage every winter, forgotten by spring.

Process, not outcome: actual pollution cuts are only 2.5% of a city's Swachh Vayu score, so Lucknow tops the rankings with PM10 over twice the safe limit. This is the blind spot of India's clean-air strategy.
GS3 · Policy design / NCAP
With actual pollution reduction worth only 2.5% of a city's Swachh Vayu score, India rewards process, not cleaner air.
Delay destroys benefits: NCAP built capacity to plan, fund and track, but ignores the cost of delay; a filter installed in 2034 cannot clean the air a child breathed in 2026.
GS3 · Economics of pollution
Delay in clean air does not postpone benefits; it destroys them.

Clean air is everyone's job: pollution comes from transport, power, industry, waste, farming and cooking, so it cannot sit with the environment ministry alone; India delivers when responsibility is clear (Ujjwala, solar).
GS2 · Coordination / GS3 governance
Clean air must be the collective responsibility of every department; Ujjwala and solar show India delivers when responsibility is clear.
NCAP 2.0 should measure exposure cut, speed of relief and who answers for missed deadlines, with central and Finance Commission grants rewarding sustained cuts.
GS3 · Way forward
NCAP 2.0 must tie funds, including Finance Commission grants, to sustained cuts in people's exposure.
keywords: Seasonal amnesia
Attention to pollution that fades after each winter
Introduction
Policy on air pollution suffers from seasonal amnesia.
Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan
Central ranking of cities on clean-air actions
Institutions
Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan rankings reward activities more than results.
Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP)
Emergency curbs in Delhi-NCR triggered by pollution levels
Delhi pollution
Despite GRAP, Delhi's winter air has not improved in four years (CREA).
Blind spot in clean-air strategy
Measuring effort instead of outcomes
Critique
The blind spot in India's clean-air strategy is measuring effort, not exposure.
Institutional fragmentation
Responsibility split across ministries and agencies
Governance challenges
Institutional fragmentation is a major obstacle to clean air across developing nations (UNEP).
NCAP 2.0
The next phase of the National Clean Air Programme
Way forward
NCAP 2.0 should shift from activity-based to outcome-based targets.
Outcome-based financing
Funds released for results, not activities
Way forward
Finance Commission grants should reward sustained cuts in pollution exposure.
Exposure reduction
Cutting the pollution people actually breathe
Metrics
Clean-air success should be judged by how much human exposure falls.
Missing the wood for the trees
Focusing on details and missing the big picture
Essay / introduction
Ranking cities on swept roads while the air stays toxic is missing the wood for the trees.
'Not another list of measures, but a stopwatch'
The writer's call for deadlines and accountability
Conclusion
India's clean-air policy needs not another list of measures, but a stopwatch.
data: South Asia's annual economic loss from air pollution, the world's heaviest
UNEP and Climate and Clean Air Coalition ('Hidden Assets'), via IE
South Asia loses the equivalent of 10% of regional GDP every year to air pollution (UNEP).
Estimated benefit of investing in 25 climate and clean-air measures (₹4 per ₹1 globally even without non-market benefits)
Every rupee spent on clean-air measures could return ₹21 in health and economic benefits (UNEP).
Weight of actual particulate reduction in a city's Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan score
Actual pollution reduction makes up only 2.5% of a city's Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan score.
Fall in Delhi-NCR's PM2.5 exposure by 2040 if standards are met on schedule from 2026; an eight-year delay halves the gain
Meeting standards on time could cut Delhi-NCR's PM2.5 exposure by 20% by 2040; an eight-year delay halves that.
examples: Lucknow, India's best million-plus city
PM10 fell from 253 to about 135 µg/m³, still over twice the national standard of 60
Rankings vs reality
Lucknow topped Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan, yet its PM10 is still more than twice the safe limit.
Delhi under GRAP
No appreciable improvement in winter air over four years (CREA)
Limits of emergency measures
Four years of GRAP have not improved Delhi's winter air, showing the limits of emergency measures.
PM Ujjwala Yojana and solar growth
India delivered at scale when responsibilities were clear
Proof of capacity
Ujjwala and solar expansion show India can deliver complex transitions when responsibility is clear.
pyqs: NCAP has been asked; NCAP 2.0 and its shift to outcomes is the natural follow-up.
WHO's stricter guidelines make India's national standard (PM10 of 60) look lax; even top-ranked Lucknow is over twice it.
Why Delhi's air is worst: winter inversion and regional sources; four years of GRAP have not fixed it.
Smog is the visible face of the seasonal crisis the writer calls 'seasonal amnesia'.
Clean air as part of the right to life under Article 21.
Waste management is part of clean air; city rankings reward such activities.

trend.t: Air pollution has been asked from many sides: the geography of Delhi's smog (GS1 2015), the right to clean air (GS2 2015), the NCAP programme (GS3 2020), WHO's air quality guidelines (2021) and photochemical smog (2022). The questions have moved from causes to programmes and standards.
trend.watch: Air pollution comes up every one or two years across GS1, GS2 and GS3. With NCAP already asked, NCAP 2.0 and outcome-based clean-air governance are must-study.
focus: NCAP 2.0: outcome-based targets, funding and accountability
Inter-departmental coordination: transport, power, industry, agriculture, waste
Health and economic costs of air pollution
Regional airsheds and Delhi-NCR: stubble, vehicles, industry

potential: The National Clean Air Programme has improved planning but not air quality. What changes should NCAP 2.0 bring to make India's clean-air policy outcome-oriented? (15 marks)
Air pollution in India is more a problem of governance than of technology. Discuss. (10 marks)
Examine the economic and health costs of air pollution in India and the case for outcome-based financing of clean-air measures. (10 marks)
Why do clean-air measures in Delhi-NCR fail to show results year after year? Suggest an inter-departmental framework. (15 marks)

practice.q: The National Clean Air Programme has improved planning but not air quality. What changes should NCAP 2.0 bring to make India's clean-air policy outcome-oriented?
parts: Introduction: NCAP and today's air (one line, with facts)
Changes NCAP 2.0 should bring (the core part)

answer.t: Launched in 2019, NCAP has built plans and budgets for polluting cities, yet even top-ranked Lucknow has PM10 over twice the safe standard, and Delhi's winter air has not improved in four years (CREA).

pts.t: Every non-attainment city now has a clean-air plan and budget.
More monitors and a public tracking system for city actions.
Central and Finance Commission grants for million-plus cities.
Rankings reward swept roads and plans; actual pollution cuts are only 2.5% of a city's score.
Action peaks in winter emergencies, then fades.
Sources lie with transport, power, industry, agriculture and households, but the job sits with environment departments.
Late action destroys benefits that cannot be recovered.
pts.ex: An eight-year delay halves Delhi-NCR's 2040 exposure gain (UNEP).

pts.t: Pollution crosses municipal and state lines.
No agency answers for missed deadlines.
Measure success by the fall in people's exposure to PM2.5, not activities.
Tie central and Finance Commission grants to sustained exposure cuts.
Give transport, power, industry, agriculture and urban departments their own targets.
Plan across states and cities that share air.
Fix timelines and name the agency answerable for each.
pts.ex: 'Not another list of measures, but a stopwatch'.

pts.t: Use health and GDP losses to prioritise spending.
pts.ex: 10% of South Asia's GDP lost each year (UNEP); ₹21 back per ₹1 invested.

pts.t: Apply the clarity that worked in Ujjwala and solar power.

answer.t: NCAP 2.0 must judge itself by the air people breathe, with every department accountable to a clock.

title: Govt notifies E100 as auto fuel for flex-fuel vehicles
syllabus: GS3 › Infrastructure: energy; Environment (pollution); Agriculture-linked industry
context: The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways amended the Central Motor Vehicle Rules to allow flex-fuel vehicles to run on up to E100 (nearly pure ethanol). Ordinary petrol or E20 vehicles cannot use E100.
ideas: Ethanol reduces dependence on imported crude oil.
GS3 · Energy security
Higher ethanol blends such as E100 cut India's dependence on imported crude.
Lower lifecycle emissions are possible, but they depend on the crop and the production process.
GS3 · Environment (balanced view)
Ethanol's climate benefit depends on the crop and process used, so lifecycle emissions must be counted.
keywords: Food vs fuel
Crops for ethanol compete with crops for food and water
Balanced view
Biofuel policy must manage the food-vs-fuel trade-off over land and water.
Flex-fuel vehicle (FFV)
Vehicle built to run on different petrol-ethanol blends
Clean transport
Flex-fuel vehicles, now allowed to run on E100, offer a parallel route to cleaner transport alongside EVs.
Lifecycle emissions
Emissions across production, transport and use
Biofuel evaluation
Judged by lifecycle emissions, not tailpipe alone, biofuels are not automatically green.
Import dependence
Reliance on imported crude oil
Energy security
Ethanol blending reduces import dependence and the oil import bill.
pyqs: Higher ethanol blends reduce dependence on imported crude.
Flex-fuel vehicles as a parallel route to cleaner transport alongside EVs.
links: Related Explained: Centre clears way for flex-fuel up to E100
summary: Flex-fuel vehicles may now run on E100, nearly pure ethanol; ordinary petrol and E20 vehicles cannot.
evolution: Ongoing debate over the use of E20 fuel (as the report notes).
E100 notified, but only for vehicles built as flex-fuel.

title: Punjab farm fires: why most stubble-burning incidents are in two districts
syllabus: GS3 › Environmental pollution; Cropping patterns; Agricultural technology · GS4 › Ethical dilemmas: private gain vs public good
context: Punjab has recorded 684 farm fires this season, 457 of them (69%) in Tarn Taran and Amritsar. Early harvesting of short-duration paddy in the Majha region lets farmers fit in a third crop of peas or potatoes before wheat, which leaves little time to clear fields without burning.
ideas: The real cause is the crop calendar, not just a lack of machines.
GS3 · Stubble burning
Stubble burning in Majha is driven by the crop calendar, not merely a lack of machines.
Fires are falling year on year; support and awareness matter as much as penalties.
GS3 policy · GS4 persuasion
Falling farm fires show that support and awareness work alongside penalties.
Leaving the paddy-wheat cycle is the long-term fix (see Manauli's sweet-corn shift).
GS3 · Crop diversification
Moving out of the paddy-wheat cycle, as Manauli did, is the long-term fix for stubble burning.
keywords: Paddy-wheat lock-in
Farmers stuck in one crop cycle by MSP and habit
Root cause
A paddy-wheat lock-in leaves farmers little choice but to burn straw before the next crop.
Negative externality
A private act that imposes costs on others
Economics of pollution
Stubble burning is a negative externality: a private saving that imposes health costs on millions.
In-situ / ex-situ residue management
Handling straw in the field / removing it for use elsewhere
Solutions
In-situ and ex-situ residue management offer alternatives to burning.
Crop diversification
Moving to a wider mix of crops
Way forward
Crop diversification is the durable answer to stubble burning and groundwater stress.
data: Farm fires by this point in the season, 2024 → 2025 → 2026
Punjab's farm fires fell from 1,857 (2024) to 743 (2025) to 684 (2026) by the same point in the season.
Despite 1.25 lakh residue-management machines, Punjab still sees farm fires.
examples: Manauli, Haryana's 'sweet corn village'
About 70% of 2,000 acres moved from paddy to sweet corn and vegetables; farmers formed an FPO
Success story
Manauli in Haryana moved about 70% of its land from paddy to sweet corn and vegetables and formed an FPO.
pyqs: Majha's third crop and Manauli's shift to sweet corn show diversification in practice.
Why farmers choose high-value crops: Manauli's returns and market links.
Farm fires and clean air: 684 fires so far against 743 last year and 1,857 in 2024.
summary: Most of Punjab's farm fires this season are in Tarn Taran and Amritsar, where a third crop leaves farmers too little time to clear fields without burning.
evolution: 1,857 fires by this point in the season.
684 fires so far, but an early spike in Majha.

title: Delhi plans a bottle-return scheme, taking a cue from Uttarakhand and Goa
syllabus: GS3 › Solid waste management; Conservation · GS4 › Environmental ethics in public administration
context: Delhi is considering a Deposit Refund Scheme (DRS) in which consumers pay an extra Re 1 or Rs 2 for a plastic bottle and get it back on return, possibly using QR codes and starting with tourist spots.
ideas: A small refundable deposit changes behaviour more than appeals alone.
GS3 · Waste management
A small refundable deposit changes behaviour more than appeals alone.
It moves people from 'use and throw' to 'use, return and recover': a circular economy.
GS3 environment · Essay
Deposit schemes move citizens from 'use and throw' to 'use, return and recover'.
Environmental ethics in public administration: the state designs incentives so that the right choice becomes the easy one.
GS4 · Environmental ethics
In a deposit scheme the state designs incentives so the environmentally right choice becomes the easy one.
keywords: Nudge
Changing behaviour through incentives, not orders
Policy design · GS4
A refundable deposit is a nudge: behaviour change without coercion.
Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR)
Producers made responsible for their products' waste
Plastic waste
Extended Producer Responsibility makes producers accountable for their plastic waste.
Circular economy
Reusing and recycling materials to cut waste
Sustainability
A circular economy keeps materials in use and cuts waste.
Deposit refund scheme
Refundable deposit on containers to encourage return
Solutions
Deposit refund schemes, as in Uttarakhand and Goa, raise container returns.
data: Bottle return rate in Uttarakhand after its deposit scheme
Uttarakhand's deposit scheme raised bottle returns from about 20% to nearly 90%.
Delhi govt report, via IE p. 11
Delhi generates about 1,500 tonnes of plastic waste a day.
examples: Kedarnath deposit refund pilot (2022)
Won a Digital India Award and was expanded across Uttarakhand
GS4
Best practice · GS4
Uttarakhand's Kedarnath deposit refund pilot (2022) won a Digital India Award and was scaled statewide.
pyqs: Directly usable: Delhi's 1,500 tonnes of plastic waste a day, 19% unprocessed, and the deposit-refund fix.
Deposit-refund schemes as a collection model: Uttarakhand's returns rose from about 20% to nearly 90%.
Use the bottle-return scheme as an environmental issue seen through environmental ethics.
summary: Delhi plans a refundable deposit on plastic bottles, copying schemes that already work in Uttarakhand and Goa.
evolution: Single-use plastic items banned across India.
Uttarakhand's pilot at Kedarnath; returns rose from about 20-22% to nearly 90%.
Goa runs a Rs 5 deposit; Delhi plans its own scheme.
